pairs.rationale: The letter names hearing, seeing and hands touching the word of life; Jesus invites seeing His hands and feet and touching Him in Luke. Both give concrete sensory testimony, without identifying the letter’s occasion or witnesses with that scene.

John places the Word with God in the beginning and says life was in Him; the letter announces manifested eternal life that was with the Father. The life and prior-with-God correspondence preserves the distinct Word, God and Father formulations.

Paul names fellowship with God’s Son Jesus Christ as the calling of the faithful God. The letter names fellowship with the Father and His Son Jesus Christ and with the announcers; the participants and announced testimony remain distinct.

Jesus gives His spoken words the purpose of His joy being in the disciples and their joy being full. The letter gives its writing the purpose of our joy being made full; the possessives and spoken/written settings remain distinct.

James associates the Father of lights with the absence of variation or shifting shadow; the letter declares God light with no darkness at all. The light and excluded shadow/darkness imagery corresponds without making the two descriptions identical.

Both passages test a claim about relationship with Him against conduct and call the contradiction a lie. Here it is fellowship while walking in darkness; there it is knowing Him without keeping His commandments. The different claims and conduct remain explicit.

Both passages attribute cleansing to Christ’s blood. Hebrews specifies cleansing the conscience from dead works to serve the living God; the letter names cleansing us from every sin while walking in light, alongside fellowship. The objects and conditions remain distinct.

Paul’s statement that all sinned supplies a concrete counterpart to the letter’s rejection of claiming to have no sin. The past sinned formulation and present have-no-sin claim are preserved, without treating them as identical grammatical statements.

The Psalm joins making sin known and confession to the Lord with divine forgiveness. The letter likewise joins confessing sins with forgiveness and cleansing, adding His faithfulness and justice. The Psalm is cited in its native Greek-based Psalm31 numbering.

Both passages use making Him a liar for rejecting God’s testimony. Here the rejected truth concerns having sinned; there unbelief rejects God’s testimony about His Son. The two specific grounds are retained without merging the cases.

Romans names Christ Jesus as the one at God’s right hand who intercedes for us; the letter names Jesus Christ the righteous as Advocate with the Father when anyone sins. Intercession and advocacy correspond without claiming the role terms are identical.

John identifies Jesus as the Lamb of God taking away the sin of the world; the letter calls Him propitiation for our sins and also for the whole world. The shared world scope preserves the distinct Lamb and propitiation formulations.

Jesus identifies having and keeping His commandments with loving Him; the letter makes keeping His commandments the test of having come to know Him. The same concrete obedience is connected with different stated predicates, love and knowledge.

Titus contrasts professing to know God with denying Him by works; the letter contrasts claiming to know Him with failing to keep His commandments and calls the claimant a liar. The conduct/profession contradiction corresponds without identifying the groups.

Jesus connects loving Him and keeping His word with the Father and Son making their dwelling with that person. The letter connects keeping His word, love of God brought to completion, and being in Him; the possessive love of God is not resolved beyond the text.

Peter presents Christ’s suffering as an example to follow in His steps. The letter makes abiding in Him entail walking as He walked. The pattern of conduct corresponds, while Peter’s specific suffering context is not made the whole meaning of walking here.

The later passage identifies the message heard from the beginning as loving one another. This verse calls the old commandment the word heard from the beginning. The repeated heard-from-the-beginning description connects the passages without inventing a dated beginning or verbatim quotation.

Jesus gives a new commandment to love one another as He loved them. The letter again calls its commandment new and places it amid light and the following brother-love teaching. The Gospel does not itself print the letter’s passing-darkness explanation.

The later passage rejects claiming love for God while hating one’s brother as a lie. Here claiming to be in light while hating one’s brother leaves one in darkness. The same brother-hatred contradicts differently stated claims.

Jesus contrasts walking in the day without stumbling through seeing light with walking at night and stumbling because light is not in that person. The letter applies light and absence of stumbling to brother-love; the journey image and ethical application remain distinct.

John says the person walking in darkness does not know where he is going. The letter repeats that concrete darkness-and-direction description and applies it to brother-hatred, adding blinded eyes. The Gospel’s immediate invitation to walk while light remains is preserved.

Peter describes believers receiving forgiveness of sins through His name; the letter tells its children their sins have been forgiven for His name’s sake. The name-related forgiveness correspondence preserves through versus for-the-sake-of wording and the distinct audiences.

Both verses address fathers as knowing Him from the beginning and young men as overcoming the evil one. The repeated statements have I write versus I have written forms; the latter adds strength, the abiding word and children knowing the Father.

The preceding I write addresses supply the repeated children, fathers and young-men pattern. This verse uses I have written, changes the children’s stated ground from forgiven sins to knowing the Father, and expands the young men’s description. No life-stage scheme is imposed.

James calls friendship with the world enmity with God; the letter prohibits love of the world and says the love of the Father is absent in the world-lover. Friendship/love and enmity/absence remain distinct, and the possessive love of the Father is not forced into one direction.

Romans forbids provision for the flesh toward its desires; the letter names desire of the flesh among what comes from the world rather than the Father. The reference supports that specific flesh-and-desire clause, without claiming Romans also prints the eyes and boastfulness clauses.

Peter contrasts grass and flower that wither and fall with the Lord’s word remaining forever. The letter contrasts the passing world and its desire with the person doing God’s will abiding forever. The fading/enduring contrast preserves the different subjects.

Both passages recall hearing that antichrist is coming and state a present reality. Here many antichrists have arisen and mark the last hour; there the antichrist spirit is already in the world. The plurality, spirit wording and last-hour conclusion remain distinct.

Paul warns that men will arise from among the hearers and draw disciples away by distorted speech; the letter describes people who went out from us and did not remain. This is a bounded comparison of departure arising within a community, without identifying the persons or occasions.

The later verse develops the received, abiding anointing and its truthful teaching. Here the anointing is from the Holy One and all of you know. The wording all of you know is preserved rather than changed to a claim of knowing all things.

The opening test says a fellowship claim combined with walking in darkness lies and does not practice the truth. This verse says the readers know the truth and no lie is from it. The truth/lie opposition corresponds without identifying every knowing claim as the earlier false claim.

The later test concerns confessing Jesus Christ come in flesh and a spirit that does not confess Jesus, called antichrist. This verse defines the liar by denying Jesus is the Christ and denying Father and Son. The distinct confession formulations are retained.

Jesus connects honoring the Son with honoring the Father and says failure to honor the Son fails to honor the sending Father. The letter connects denying or confessing the Son with not having or having the Father. Honor and confession are related but not substituted as identical words.

Second John connects abiding in Christ’s teaching with having both Father and Son. Here the word heard from the beginning abiding in the readers leads to their abiding in the Son and Father. The teaching/word and having/abiding formulations remain distinct.

Titus places hope in eternal life promised by God who does not lie before the ages; this verse identifies the promise He Himself promised us as eternal life. The promised-life correspondence retains the stated time and divine description supplied only by Titus.

The nearby denial of Jesus as Christ and of Father and Son, followed by the denial/confession distinction, gives specific doctrinal content alongside this warning about people leading the readers astray. The warning does not supply names or authorize identifying contemporary individuals.

Jesus says the Holy Spirit will teach the disciples all things and remind them of what He said. The letter describes the received anointing as teaching about all things truthfully and calls readers to abide. The anointing is not silently replaced with the Gospel’s explicit Spirit noun, nor read as universal personal omniscience.

Colossians says that when Christ, your life, is revealed, believers will also be revealed with Him in glory; the letter joins His being manifested and His coming with confidence rather than shrinking in shame. The related revealed/manifested wording preserves the distinct glory and confidence consequences and supplies no date.

The later verse says the person practicing righteousness is righteous just as He is righteous. This verse connects knowing His righteousness with the righteous practitioner’s having been born of Him. The shared righteousness/practice comparison preserves the additional birth claim and does not resolve an unprinted pronoun identity.
